bearings.paper_claim: In the 107th House roll-call matrix (990 votes, 2001-02) the leading SVD coordinate is the bipartisan one, which groups nearly all members together. It holds 45.3% of the sum of squares, against 29.6% for the partisan coordinate. Always guessing 'pass' is right on 735 of 990 votes (74.2%). The Optimal Classification comparison keeps 749 of 990 roll calls after dropping votes with a small minority share; the threshold glyph is lost in extraction.
bearings.paper_location: Voting Patterns, PNAS pp 7059-7061, Eqs 1-3, Figs 3-4, Table 2 caption
bearings.system_side: Path V counts a category as corroborated when a member's mean signed lean is at least 0.5 with n at least 1 (moneyball_core.py:871). build_vote_category.py aggregates direction times Yea(+1)/Nay(-1) over every Yea or Nay member vote on HS117, HS118 and HS119 roll calls, with no contestedness or minority-share filter (grep found none). One Yea on a lopsided roll call alone gives lean 1.0 with n=1 and passes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Paper supports only that bipartisan variance dominates the 107th House matrix. Its 45.3% is for all 990 votes in 2001-02, not a 117-119 statistic and not a share of lopsided votes in CU data. The share of admitted roll calls with minority at or below a small threshold is unmeasured; this is a candidate check, UNVERIFIED until reproduced (DE-062). The code read does not establish that the source is final-passage only.
bearings.verifier_note: Code side and all paper numbers reproduced. Softened because the 45.3% transfer to the CU vote data is a candidate, not a finding. Rank-honors and grade feeds (votes 0.4) not located by grep and left unverified.

bearings.paper_claim: In the 107th House the four Intelligence subcommittees each include at least half of the 20-member parent committee and at least one third of each other subcommittee, with normalized interlocks of 14.4 to 26.6 among the five nodes. Single-linkage clustering places subcommittees at the bottom of a roughly four-level hierarchy (subcommittees, committees, groups, House).
bearings.paper_location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p7057; Structure of the House, p7059, Figs 1-2
bearings.system_side: seat_weights gives each subcommittee seat BASE tier times SUBF (1/6) membership (committee_scores.py:126, 161), and subcommittee leadership multiplies that seat's membership by Chair sub 7.5 or Ranking sub 4.5 (lines 127-129, 169). compute sums seat values as independent additive units (lines 173-183).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The nesting evidence is one parent committee in one Congress, so it cannot support a general statement that subcommittee seats are nested in the parent. The paper calls these overlaps expected and measures membership redundancy, not influence, so it says nothing on whether additive counting is wrong for CU outcomes. The 1/6 factor is a code constant; its origin as owner judgment is not shown in the lines read.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper figures and code lines reproduced. Softened because the summary generalizes one committee example to subcommittee membership largely sitting inside the parent. The 'owner judgment' label for 1/6 was not found in the code read.

bearings.paper_claim: Committees differ in mean partisan extremism of their members. Select Homeland Security ranks 4th of 113 committees and above all 19 standing committees. Rules is the second most extreme standing committee (after Judiciary) and 18th of 113. Intelligence and its four subcommittees rank among the 10 least extreme of 113.
bearings.paper_location: Voting Patterns, PNAS p7061-7062, lines 483-500; Fig 2 colour coding p7059
bearings.system_side: The committee score depends only on the CU tier base (Highly 3.0, Moderately 1.8, Slightly 0.9) and leadership role. seat_weights and compute take no input about partisan composition or extremism of members.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Extremism is relative to the 107th House mean, tracks party, and is descriptive with no test. It is evidence of heterogeneity across committees, not a weight to adopt. Any use would mix party loyalty with CU leverage, the chicken-or-egg problem Paul raised.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side fully reproduced. Code side checked for seat_weights and compute only. The summary claim that the party elite bonus is display-only was not checked.

bearings.paper_claim: Porter et al. project a two-mode representative-by-committee assignment network onto committees, weighting each committee pair by observed shared members over the count expected under random same-size assignment (1 = chance). The structure result uses assignment data only. The political-correlation result uses roll-call votes, so it is not free of political information.
bearings.paper_location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p7057; Voting Patterns, PNAS p7059-7060
bearings.system_side: load_network reads the newest congress_cosponsor network (or holistic or sector cosponsor families) and mean-symmetrizes it. The multilayer builder adds press engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance layers. grep over fec/network and fec/engine found no committee co-membership or interlock layer; the only committee hit in fec/network is a label in process_quorum.py.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No committee co-membership layer exists, so any such layer would be new and unvalidated. Its observed/expected weighting must not be applied to cosponsor edges, which was measured and rejected (brain topic note, line 101, per-edge normalization REJECTED). The item's Paul-annotation entries link Porter to a committee layer, not to the cosponsor graph.
bearings.verifier_note: Code claims reproduced. Paper claim softened because the paper does use roll-call votes for its second result. The analyst's statement that Paul's component cites Porter for the cosponsor graph is not supported by Paul's annotation entries.

bearings.paper_claim: Porter et al. normalize shared membership against the count expected if same-size committees were assigned at random (normalized interlock, 1 = chance), so container size does not by itself produce strong ties. The paper does not claim that raw shared membership is uninformative.
bearings.paper_location: Networks of Committees, PNAS p7057 (normalized interlock definition, lines 82-92)
bearings.system_side: closeness_math.py: peer exposure adds duration divided by max(1, count-1) raised to gamma (line 83); member exposure adds duration divided by max(1, count) raised to gamma (line 84); _at divides by max(1, count-1) for peers (line 92). Larger concurrent headcount dilutes pairwise exposure. employment_history.py line 83 records admin containers carrying 70.8% of co-tenure pairs in the v5 generation. The r = 0.87 artifact figure was not found in fec/staffer_network.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Porter's normalization is an observed-over-expected ratio at the container level. The Melange dilution is a duration-weighted 1/n^gamma on person-person exposure. Different unit and functional form, and Porter gives no basis for the exponent. The output is exposure, not closeness or access (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Code reproduced. Paper claim overstated: Porter does not say raw membership is uninformative. The r = 0.87 figure is unverified in the repo.

summary_issues: Says Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees. The paper says second most extreme (after Judiciary). Clarify the direction.
Says subcommittee membership largely sits inside the parent committee. The paper gives one example (Intelligence, each subcommittee at least half of the parent) for one Congress.

Says two components cite Porter for community structure. In the repo the template cites Sotoudeh-Porter-Krishnagopal at line 738 and no Porter 2005 or Porter-Mucha-Newman string exists in fec/. The component-record wording was not located, so this stays unverified.
Describes Porter's SVD as a NOMINATE-class method (rel flags). Porter uses an unnormalized SVD benchmarked against Optimal Classification; it is not DW-NOMINATE. Reword.
Says the say-do vote evidence is final-passage. The producer aggregates all Yea or Nay member votes on HS117-119 roll calls linked to bills, with no final-passage filter seen. Clarify.

Says Paul's component position cites Porter as grounding the cosponsor graph. Paul's annotation entries link Porter only to a committee or multi-layer committee network (inferred). Unsupported as stated.

Cites a staffer artifact with r = 0.87 and a 70.8 percent admin-container share. The 70.8 percent appears in employment_history.py line 83; the r = 0.87 figure is not in the repo. Mark as artifact-sourced.
Says Melange has no committee co-membership layer. Verified: none found in fec/network or fec/engine; committees enter only through committee_scores.py.
Paul's paraphrase (two-mode committee network plus one-mode representative network) is a misreading: the paper projects only committees. Verified against lines 76-79.
Paper says no significance test or randomization null for any value; the summary's 'the conclusion is not random' is descriptive and should carry that label.
